phases.title: GPU, CPU and the machine stack
Inference engineering: from silicon to serving

A1.title: AWS From Scratch
A1.why: Eight mechanism families in pure Python, 18 checks. The best first course: no dependencies, every stage is a real failure mode.

stages.title: explicit deny > allow > implicit deny
stages.action: IAM: an explicit Deny wins; otherwise any matching Allow applies; otherwise implicit Deny.
stages.predict: the result when Allow and Deny both match.

stages.title: conditions and permissions boundaries
stages.action: Evaluate conditions and permissions boundaries — a boundary only SHRINKS the permission, it can never grant one.
stages.predict: Allow outside the boundary.

stages.title: STS assume-role: both directions
stages.action: Assume-role needs trust on both sides: the caller may assume, AND the role must allow the action.
stages.predict: identity policy Allows but trust policy does not.

stages.title: objects, ETags and multipart
stages.action: Objects carry an ETag (MD5 simple, part-hash multipart); multipart assembles the parts in order.
stages.predict: the ETag of a two-part multipart upload.

stages.title: prefix listing and delete markers
stages.action: Listing uses prefix + delimiter; a delete marker HIDES a version without destroying it.
stages.predict: what GET returns after a delete marker is added.

stages.title: visibility timeout and redelivery
stages.action: The visibility timeout hides a message; if it is not deleted in time it is redelivered.
stages.predict: whether the same message is received twice.

stages.title: dead letters, FIFO and dedup
stages.action: DLQ after max receives; FIFO orders by message group and dedups by id within a window.
stages.predict: how many times a failing message is delivered.

stages.title: composite keys, query, conditions
stages.action: DynamoDB composite key = partition + sort: Query is within one partition, and conditional writes fail cleanly on conflict.
stages.predict: whether Query can span partitions.

stages.title: capacity, hot partitions, scan cost
stages.action: Capacity: RCU/WCU from item size; a hot partition is a bad key distribution; Scan costs roughly the whole table.
stages.predict: WCU for a 2KB write with no batching.

stages.title: cold starts and warm state
stages.action: Lambda cold start initialises the container once; warm invocations reuse whatever the container kept in memory.
stages.predict: how many inits over six invocations.

stages.title: concurrency, reservations, async retry
stages.action: Reserved concurrency caps a function; an async invoke retries twice and then goes to the DLQ.
stages.predict: attempts for a failing async handler.

stages.title: fanout and filter policies
stages.action: SNS fans out; filter policies match message attributes (AND within a key, OR across values).
stages.predict: which subscriptions a two-attribute message hits.

stages.title: EventBridge pattern matching
stages.action: EventBridge patterns match nested detail; arrays mean OR, and an EMPTY pattern matches everything.
stages.predict: whether {} matches a random event.

stages.title: envelope encryption
stages.action: KMS envelope encryption: a data key encrypts the data, and the CMK encrypts the data key.
stages.predict: what you must store alongside the ciphertext.

stages.title: encryption context and rotation
stages.action: Encryption context must match on decrypt; rotation changes the CMK but old ciphertext still decrypts.
stages.predict: decrypt with a mismatched context.

stages.title: CIDR, subnets and longest-prefix routing
stages.action: VPC: CIDR -> subnets, and routes pick the LONGEST matching prefix, not the first or the shortest.
stages.predict: which route wins for 10.0.1.5.

stages.title: stateful SG vs stateless NACL
stages.action: Security groups are STATEFUL (return traffic is automatic); NACLs are STATELESS (allow both directions explicitly).
stages.predict: why a NACL blocks the reply to an allowed request.

stages.title: the pipeline, and its failures
stages.action: Capstone: wire the services into one pipeline and reproduce each of its failure modes deliberately.
stages.predict: which service's failure stops the pipeline first.

A2.title: LLM From Scratch
A2.why: BPE, attention, sampling, KV cache, RoPE. 13 checks, pure Python.

stages.title: pair counts and non-overlapping merges
stages.action: Write get_pair_counts as a dict of adjacent pairs, then merge_pair with an index that SKIPS PAST each merge, so [1,1,1] becomes [9,1] and not two overlapping merges.
stages.predict: In [1,1,1,2], how many adjacent (1,1) pairs? (two, not three)

stages.title: deterministic training and compression
stages.action: In train_bpe, take the most frequent pair but break ties by the smallest pair, and start new ids at 256. Determinism is the whole point — same corpus, same table.
stages.predict: Train twice on one corpus: identical merge table?

stages.title: rank-ordered encode and round-trip
stages.action: Make encode repeatedly apply the LOWEST-RANK merge anywhere in the sequence (not a left-to-right sweep); decode expands ids bottom-up.

stages.title: stable softmax
stages.action: In softmax, subtract the row max before exp: exp(x - max). The result is identical and can never overflow.
stages.predict: softmax([1000,1001]) — finite, and sums to 1.

stages.title: attention weights and the causal mask
stages.action: Apply the causal mask as -inf BEFORE the softmax, so each row still sums to 1 and position 0 attends only to itself.
stages.predict: the output row for position 0 equals V[0].

stages.title: temperature and hard greedy
stages.action: temperature 0 is hard greedy: one-hot at the argmax, -inf everywhere else. Temperature divides the logits.
stages.predict: sample(temp=0) is deterministic — the tail can never fire.

stages.title: top-k
stages.action: top_k keeps the k largest and breaks ties by smallest index, keeping BOTH tied values.
stages.predict: top-2 of [1,3,3,2] keeps indices 1 and 2.

stages.title: top-p keeps the crossing token
stages.action: top_p keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches p, INCLUDING the token that crosses it (>= not >).
stages.predict: [.5,.3,.15,.05] at p=.9 keeps the .15 token.

stages.title: seeded sampling is reproducible
stages.action: Thread the Random instance you were handed through every sampling call; never touch the global random module.
stages.predict: one seed twice gives the same 50 samples.

stages.title: cache append and shape
stages.action: KVCache stores parallel key/value lists; append, and make len/keys/values reflect exactly what was appended.
stages.predict: the length after two appends.

stages.title: cached output is bit-exact
stages.action: cached_step must reproduce recompute_step to <1e-9: append the new K/V and attend over ALL cached rows — read the cache.
stages.predict: dropping the last key must change the output.

stages.title: the cost model: linear vs quadratic
stages.action: Count interactions: recompute is O(t*d) per step (quadratic overall), the cache is O(d) plus the append (linear).
stages.predict: doubling the prompt multiplies prefill work by ~4.

stages.title: norm and relative-position invariants
stages.action: Rotate each (x2i, x2i+1) pair by pos*freq; check the norm is preserved and dot(q@p, k@p+d) ignores p entirely.
stages.predict: the relative dot product is identical for every p.

A3.title: Context Caching From Scratch
A3.why: The direct continuation of A2: page, prefix-share, evict the KV cache without changing the output. 16 checks.

stages.title: linear algebra helpers
stages.action: Implement the plain-list vector helpers (dot, softmax, matmul) first — everything above is built from them.
stages.predict: the shape of a 2x3 times 3x2 result.

stages.title: KVCache append/truncate/clone
stages.action: append/truncate/clone must keep keys and values aligned; clone must deep-copy rows, not share them.
stages.predict: mutating a clone leaves the original untouched.

stages.title: cached == uncached attention
stages.action: Cached attention must equal uncached attention within tolerance — append the new K/V and attend over all rows.
stages.predict: the max difference between cached and uncached.

stages.title: prefill and the cost model
stages.action: Prefill is quadratic in prompt length; decode is linear. Count multiply-adds to make the difference concrete.
stages.predict: the ratio of prefill work at 128 vs 64 tokens.

stages.title: layer_norm and gelu
stages.action: layer_norm needs a variance epsilon; gelu uses the tanh approximation. Match the checker's tolerance exactly.
stages.predict: layer_norm of a constant vector.

stages.title: generation matches exactly
stages.action: Generation with the cache must be token-identical to the no-cache path — same logits, same argmax.
stages.predict: the generated token sequence with and without cache.

stages.title: truncate, clone, prefix reuse
stages.action: truncate must cut keys and values together; clone must not share rows; prefix reuse must not mutate the source request.
stages.predict: reusing a prefix twice gives the same continuation.

stages.title: block hashing and chaining
stages.action: Hash each token block, then CHAIN: the child's hash includes the parent's, so identical prefixes share one key.
stages.predict: do two prompts sharing a prefix produce one shared block?

stages.title: matching, eviction, isolation
stages.action: Match the longest cached prefix, evict by policy, and keep per-request isolation — one request must not evict another's pinned blocks.
stages.predict: the hit length for a prompt sharing 2 of 3 blocks.

stages.title: matching and node splitting
stages.action: Radix matching walks edge labels and SPLITS a node when a prefix ends mid-edge — test the split explicitly.
stages.predict: the tree shape after inserting 'abc' then 'abd'.

stages.title: eviction and pinning
stages.action: Evict leaves first; pinned nodes are exempt. Walk to find a valid victim rather than evicting the root.
stages.predict: which node is evicted when all are leaves.

stages.title: block allocation and growth
stages.action: The block allocator hands out fixed-size blocks and grows the block table; track free/used and refcounts.
stages.predict: how many blocks a 17-token sequence with block=8 needs.

stages.title: forking and copy-on-write
stages.action: fork shares blocks by reference (refcount++); a WRITE to a shared block copies it first (refcount--, new block).
stages.predict: does writing to a fork change the parent's tokens?

stages.title: exact and semantic caching
stages.action: Exact cache first, then a semantic threshold — tune it so near-duplicates hit but distinct prompts miss.
stages.predict: whether a reworded question should be a hit.

stages.title: cache-aware routing
stages.action: Route each request to the replica that already holds its prefix; fall back to least-loaded when nobody does.
stages.predict: the hit rate after routing vs round-robin.

stages.title: capstone: identical output
stages.action: Capstone: wire prefix + paged + semantic caches together and keep the output identical to the uncached model.
stages.predict: compute saved (%) and whether output is bit-identical.

A4.title: ContextCite From Scratch
A4.why: Which context caused the answer — ablation and a LASSO surrogate. The eval-flavoured course, and the bridge into RAG. 14 checks.

stages.title: splitting text into sources
stages.action: Split text into sources with offsets precise enough to rebuild the full context byte-for-byte.
stages.predict: the number of sources in a 3-sentence passage.

stages.title: rebuilding ablated contexts
stages.action: Rebuild the ablated context from a kept-source mask, preserving order and spacing exactly.
stages.predict: the context when only source 2 is kept.

stages.title: logit-prob math and stability
stages.action: logit-prob = logit[target] - logsumexp(logits); subtract the max inside logsumexp so it never overflows.
stages.predict: log-prob of a token with logit 0 among [0,0,0].

stages.title: aggregation and response score
stages.action: Aggregate per-token logit-probs into one response score — pick sum or mean and apply it consistently.
stages.predict: sum vs mean on a 4-token response.

stages.title: sampling the design matrix
stages.action: Sample a binary design matrix over sources; each row is a kept/dropped subset of the context.
stages.predict: how many distinct rows a 5-source sampler can produce.

stages.title: soft threshold and standardising
stages.action: Coordinate-descent LASSO: soft-threshold each coordinate and standardise inputs so the penalty is comparable across sources.
stages.predict: soft_threshold(0.5, 1.0).

stages.title: recovering a known sparse signal
stages.action: Fit should recover a known sparse signal — check the support and the coefficient signs against ground truth.
stages.predict: which coefficients are exactly zero.

stages.title: end-to-end attribution
stages.action: End-to-end: abduction (drop sources) -> design matrix -> LASSO -> per-source attribution scores.
stages.predict: the coefficient on the source the answer actually needs.

stages.title: span attribution, zero extra calls
stages.action: Span attribution reuses the same ablation samples — assert the number of model calls does NOT grow with span count.
stages.predict: model calls with 1 source vs 4 spans.

stages.title: spearman rank correlation
stages.action: Spearman: rank both vectors and correlate the ranks; assign average ranks on ties.
stages.predict: Spearman of a perfectly reversed ranking.

stages.title: held-out LDS and top-k drop
stages.action: Held-out LDS and top-k drop: measure whether the surrogate predicts on ablations it never saw.
stages.predict: LDS of a perfect ranker.

stages.title: verification and pruning
stages.action: Applications: verify a claim by ablation, and prune sources the surrogate calls dead.
stages.predict: whether removing the top source flips the answer.

stages.title: detecting a poisoned source
stages.action: Detect a poisoned source: its coefficient should dominate, and no honest source should be a perfect predictor.
stages.predict: the coefficient profile with one injected source.

stages.title: leave-one-out fails on redundancy
stages.action: Leave-one-out fails under redundancy — two identical sources split the credit and each looks unimportant. Reproduce it.
stages.predict: each duplicate's leave-one-out score.

A5.title: System Design
A5.why: Optional but cheap: caching, queues, idempotency, rate limiting. Makes sqs/dynamodb in A1 click and underpins the agent half.

A6.title: Dynamo From Scratch
A6.why: The paper behind DynamoDB, in depth: quorums, hinted handoff, Merkle anti-entropy. 17 checks.

stages.title: ring: add/remove/coordinator
stages.action: Ring: place a node's tokens, find a key's successor clockwise, and remove the node's tokens when it leaves.
stages.predict: who coordinates a key between two nodes.

stages.title: preference lists (N distinct nodes)
stages.action: preference_list walks virtual tokens clockwise and must SKIP nodes already chosen, returning N DISTINCT nodes.
stages.predict: N when the ring has fewer than N nodes.

stages.title: load balance and key migration
stages.action: Adding/removing a node should move about 1/N of the keys; measure balance as max/min load across nodes.
stages.predict: the fraction of keys that move when one node joins.

stages.title: strategy 3: fixed partitions
stages.action: Strategy 3: fixed partitions (a fixed Q), each node owns several — routing is a table lookup, not a ring walk.
stages.predict: how key movement compares to the ring.

stages.title: clock ordering and merge
stages.action: Vector clocks compare pointwise: equal, descendant, ancestor, or concurrent — get all four cases right.
stages.predict: the relation between {A:1} and {A:1,B:1}.

stages.title: reconciliation (paper Figure 3)
stages.action: On conflicting siblings, reconcile with the paper's rule and MERGE the clocks so the result dominates both.
stages.predict: the merged clock of two concurrent writes.

stages.title: clock truncation
stages.action: Truncate the clock by dropping the oldest entries when it exceeds the cap, keeping recent causality.
stages.predict: which entries survive a cap of 2.

stages.title: storage node keeps siblings
stages.action: A storage node keeps the value plus all its siblings; a read returns every sibling, not just the newest.
stages.predict: the sibling count after two concurrent writes.

stages.title: N/R/W put and get
stages.action: N/R/W put and get: write to N preference nodes, read from R, and R+W>N is what guarantees overlap.
stages.predict: whether R=1,W=1,N=3 can read a stale value.

stages.title: siblings and read repair
stages.action: Reads collect siblings from R nodes; read repair pushes the newest value back to the stale replicas it saw.
stages.predict: which replicas get repaired on a read.

stages.title: sloppy quorum writes a hint
stages.action: Sloppy quorum: when a preference node is down, write to the next live node and store a HINT saying where it belongs.
stages.predict: hint count after one node is down.

stages.title: hinted handoff delivery
stages.action: Deliver hints when the owner returns, then delete the local copy — delivery must be idempotent.
stages.predict: what happens if the same hint is delivered twice.

stages.title: merkle tree build and diff
stages.action: Merkle tree: hash leaves (key ranges), hash pairs upward; the diff walks only branches whose hashes differ.
stages.predict: how many nodes one changed key dirties.

stages.title: anti-entropy is a union
stages.action: Anti-entropy is a UNION of values, reconciled with the same clock logic — not blind last-write-wins.
stages.predict: the value after syncing two divergent replicas.

stages.title: gossip convergence O(log S)
stages.action: Gossip converges in O(log S): each round every node tells a few peers; track rounds to full knowledge.
stages.predict: rounds for 64 nodes to all learn one fact.

stages.title: local failure detection, seeds
stages.action: Failure detection is local (heartbeat + suspicion), and seeds are how a brand-new node joins without a full member list.
stages.predict: how a node is declared dead with no central registry.

stages.title: capstone: cart + availability
stages.action: Capstone: run the cart workload against the full cluster and hit the stated availability target.
stages.predict: successful-write rate under 30% node churn.

A7.title: Deploy & Debug
A7.why: Capacity math, SLOs, root-causing faults from metrics. The operations thread that every later course leans on. 12 checks.

stages.title: KV cache and batch-size math
stages.action: KV cache bytes/token = 2 * layers * KV_HEADS * head_dim * bytes. Using query heads sizes the fleet 4x too large.
stages.predict: bytes/token for Llama-3-8B (8 KV heads).

stages.title: fleet sizing and quorum tolerance
stages.action: Size the fleet from concurrency and tokens/s, then subtract the failure tolerance R+W>N implies.
stages.predict: how many nodes can die and quorum still hold.

stages.title: percentiles and summaries
stages.action: Percentiles are not averages: sort and take the rank. p99 is where the outliers live.

stages.title: queueing and fan-out tails
stages.action: Little's law and fan-out: one slow dependency multiplies the tail across parallel calls.
stages.predict: tail latency with 10 parallel 100ms calls.

stages.title: SLOs, budgets and burn rate
stages.action: SLO is an objective over a window; error budget = 1 - SLO; burn rate is how fast you are spending it.
stages.predict: the error budget for 99.9% over 30 days.

stages.title: diagnose 6 serving faults
stages.action: Map each fault to its metric signature: KV full -> cache-miss spike; overload -> queue growth.
stages.predict: the signature of a full KV cache.

stages.title: undersized KV vs overload
stages.action: Undersized KV and overload look similar — separate them by cache-hit rate and memory, not latency alone.
stages.predict: which metric distinguishes the two.

stages.title: diagnose 5 store faults
stages.action: Store faults: node down, hint backlog, and gossip disagreement each have a distinct fingerprint.
stages.predict: the fingerprint of hinted-handoff backlog.

stages.title: node down vs strict quorum
stages.action: Node down with QUORUM MET (hint backlog) differs from STRICT-quorum failure (write errors).
stages.predict: which one still serves reads.

stages.title: liveness vs readiness probes
stages.action: Liveness RESTARTS a hung process; readiness REMOVES it from the load balancer. Do not confuse the two.
stages.predict: what a failing readiness probe does.

stages.title: canary analysis and staging
stages.action: Canary: compare canary against control on the same traffic, with enough samples to see the effect.
stages.predict: whether 90 samples can detect a 2% regression.

stages.title: budget-based auto-rollback
stages.action: Auto-rollback on burn-rate, not a single blip — a 30-second spike must not page.
stages.predict: whether a 30s spike trips a 1h-budget alarm.

A8.title: Autograd From Scratch
A8.why: Built: the engine every training course in this repository assumes — reverse-mode automatic differentiation over exact rationals, on a provided forward algebra (`exact.py`) so the gradients are yours: the graph and its topological order, the local derivatives, broadcasting and the reduction of a broadcast gradient, accumulation, the seed of a non-scalar output, detach, the kink at a tie, the exact finite-difference oracle, and one training step. Ten checks and 504 planted mutations, no float anywhere — every gradient is an equal pair and the last stage reproduces a reference gradient exactly.

stages.title: The graph and the order
stages.predict: Why a diamond-shaped graph visited without a topological order returns the right answer on a tree and the wrong one — or never returns — on a diamond.

stages.title: The local derivatives
stages.predict: What `d(a/b)/db` is, and why implementing division as `a * pow(b, -1)` is not the same function on the integers.

stages.title: Broadcasting and the reduction
stages.action: Write `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `sum` and `mean` over operands of different shapes in stage_03.py.
stages.predict: What shape the gradient of a `(4,)` operand is when it was added to a `(3, 4)`, and what `mean`'s gradient is missing when every element is the same.

stages.title: The chain rule through a matrix
stages.predict: Which operand's gradient is `G·Bᵀ` and which is `Aᵀ·G`, and why swapping them is invisible on a square symmetric fixture.

stages.title: Accumulation and reuse
stages.predict: What a second `backward()` without `zero_grad()` does to a gradient, and what a node used twice should receive.

stages.title: The seed of a non-scalar output
stages.action: Write `backward` with a seed and `sum_to_scalar` in stage_06.py.
stages.predict: What a `(2,)` output's backward needs that a scalar's does not, and what number the engine silently uses if you leave it out.

stages.title: Detach, and the graph that must not grow
stages.predict: What a detach must drop so the backward cannot reach through it, and why an inference pass that builds a graph costs memory it never uses.

stages.title: The kink
stages.predict: Where the gradient of a tied `max` goes under this course's convention, and what `relu'(0)` must be for that convention to hold in every call.

stages.title: The oracle
stages.predict: Which polynomial's central difference is exactly its derivative for every step, and what a cubic's difference is off by.

stages.title: The capstone: the step
stages.predict: How many exact steps the 2→4→1 model needs to learn XOR, and why two hundred of them are not writable.

B1.title: RAG From Scratch
B1.why: Built and ready: chunking, TF-IDF, a vector index, BM25, rank fusion, reranking, citations, tenant isolation, recall@k. 9 checks.

stages.title: chunking with exact offsets
stages.action: Implement chunk(): stride = size - overlap, emit {start, end, text} until the text is covered, keep the last chunk short and the offsets exact.
stages.predict: How many chunks for a 10-char text, size 4, overlap 1?

stages.title: TF-IDF on sparse dicts
stages.action: Implement tokenize, Tfidf.fit/transform (smoothed idf, L2 normalise) and cosine over sparse dicts.
stages.predict: What is cosine(v, v) for a TF-IDF vector, and why not exactly 1?

stages.title: exact brute-force vector index
stages.action: Implement VectorIndex with insertion order preserved and a stable tie-break, so equal scores are deterministic.
stages.predict: With two docs scoring 1.0 and 0.5, what does search(q, 2) return?

stages.title: BM25
stages.action: Implement bm25_scores: smoothed non-negative idf, length-normalised tf, one score per document.
stages.predict: For a term absent from every document, what is its contribution?

stages.title: reciprocal rank fusion
stages.action: Implement RRF over rank lists: score += 1/(k + rank), deduped, sorted by score with a stable tie-break.
stages.predict: Which doc wins: #1 dense + #2 lexical, or #3 dense + #1 lexical?

stages.title: reranking and MRR
stages.action: Implement query-coverage scoring, rerank the candidate list, and mrr() to measure the move.
stages.predict: MRR of relevant doc at rank 2 before, and rank 1 after rerank?

stages.title: citations and unsupported claims
stages.action: Implement find_support and unsupported with a coverage threshold, so ungrounded claims are flagged not printed.
stages.predict: A claim matching 2 of 3 tokens: supported at threshold 0.6?

stages.title: tenant isolation
stages.action: Implement TenantIndex so search scopes to the tenant before scoring; an unknown tenant returns [].
stages.predict: Can a search for tenant A ever return a tenant-B key?

stages.title: end-to-end retrieval and recall@k
stages.action: Wire stages 1-3 into build/retrieve and measure recall@k against a tiny labelled set.
stages.predict: Recall@1 for three questions whose gold docs are unambiguous?

B2.title: Vector Index From Scratch
B2.why: Brute force -> IVF -> HNSW, with recall and work measured against the exact index you built in B1. 10 checks, pure Python, and the stage that makes 'approximate' mean something.

stages.title: the exact baseline and recall@k
stages.action: Implement dot, ExactIndex (stable ties, a work counter, copies of the vectors) and recall_at_k.
stages.predict: Two relevant documents, one of them in the top 1: recall@1?

stages.title: the metric, and the norm cache
stages.action: Implement norm, l2, cosine (0.0 for a zero vector) and CosineIndex with each stored vector's norm cached at add time.
stages.predict: Cosine of a long vector and a short one in the same direction?

stages.title: k-means, the partition IVF scans
stages.action: Implement squared_l2, assign and kmeans with k-means++ init from random.Random(seed), stopping when assignments stop changing.
stages.predict: Which point does k-means++ pick as the second centroid?

stages.title: IVF: probing and ranking across lists
stages.action: Implement IVFIndex: partition with k-means, probe the nprobe nearest centroids, score only their members, rank the union.
stages.predict: With nprobe=nlist, how does the answer compare to the exact one?

stages.title: the frontier, and the query set
stages.action: Implement sweep, tune_nprobe and report: recall against the exact index, tuned on one query set and measured on another.
stages.predict: Tuned on one set, measured on another: which number is bigger?

stages.title: the HNSW graph, built not searched
stages.action: Implement build, neighbors, level and layers: geometric levels, mutual links, degree caps at layer 0 and above.
stages.predict: What fraction of 120 nodes ends up above layer 0?

stages.title: the walk, and ef
stages.action: Implement search: greedy descent above layer 0, a best-first walk with a pool of ef at layer 0, the k best rows seen.
stages.predict: Mean recall@10 at ef=8 and ef=96 over 25 queries?

stages.title: deletions without unlink
stages.action: Implement DeletableIndex: tombstone on delete, filter during the walk so the pool still fills, re-admit on add.
stages.predict: Delete 25 of 60 nodes: how many rows does k=35 return?

stages.title: int8 quantization
stages.action: Implement ScalarQuantizer (per-dimension fit, clamp, dequantize) and QuantizedIndex scoring the exact query against the reconstructed vector.
stages.predict: Codes for a corpus spanning [0,1], given a query at 1000?

stages.title: the frontier, and choosing a point on it
stages.action: Implement compare (recall, bytes, work per index, tuned by the caller) and choose: the fewest bytes that meet the floor.
stages.predict: Recall floor 0.9 and a 4-bytes-per-vector index at recall 0.5: which index is chosen?

C1.title: Evals From Scratch
C1.why: Datasets, exact/F1 metrics, LLM-as-judge and its calibration, statistical significance, regression gating. Do this before agents.

stages.title: the eval set, and the split that must not leak
stages.action: Implement load() with validation and copies, and split() that keeps whole groups on one side of the split, seeded.

F1.title: Benchmark From Scratch (Mus)

The game is provided (`mus.py`: a Fournier mus table with the four lances, three bet scales and two reference seats); the measurement is the exercise. Reference repo: ~/Desarrollo/mus-benchmark.

G3.title: CPU From Scratch
G3.why: Ten stages, all graded, on a provided ISA and assembler (`isa.py`: 29 opcodes in the same family as G1's — 32-bit words, 16 registers, [opcode:6][rd:4][rs1:4][rs2:4][imm:14], plus the memory sizes, the compares and the flags a datapath needs). Mask a word and derive the flags; decode an encoding whose unused fields must not become operands; keep a register file whose zero register cannot be written and whose snapshots are copies; divide and take remainders the way hardware does rather than the way Python does; address bytes with alignment and bounds checked before anything is stored; fetch and execute with a fault as data and a trace of effects; then run the same programs on a five-stage pipeline that must retire the identical trace — stalling at first, then forwarding with the one-cycle load-use stall and a branch flush — before measuring both machines and reporting the CPI. One program, two machines, one result.

G4.title: OS From Scratch
G4.why: Built, and the salvage is part of it: `linux-from-scratch/` (the curriculum kept from the branch) is the prose, and ten graded stages are the course, on a provided machine (`machine.py`, `devices.py`, `userland.py`) whose promises break as soon as a program does something it should not. The thesis: an operating system is what you write after the hardware breaks your last promise. Join a boot map's regions and derive the frames a kernel may hand out; allocate frames from a bitmap that protects the frame its own bits live in and answers all or nothing; build page tables whose entries can never be read as frame numbers and check a permission bit on every walk, not just on the first; take a fault as a word a handler decides from rather than an exception; check a pointer before it is used and write the line that promises the act before the act; make a process a dict with a space, a ledger and a zombie at the end, and `fork` copy frames rather than table entries; pick by priority and age behind a quantum that rotates; put two CPUs on an interleaving where the critical section is a lock whose order is checked; format a real on-disk filesystem whose superblock is written last and mount only what a barrier made durable; and end on a userland whose kernel report is recomputed from its own log and cross-checked, key by key, against the machine's records.

stages.title: The trap table, and the fault as data

stages.title: The syscall boundary, and the pointer you did not check
stages.predict: What a kernel has to know about a pointer before it may read through it, and why the line about a call is written before the call rather than after it.

stages.title: The process, and the frame nobody gave back

stages.title: The scheduler, and the wakeup that never came

stages.title: Two CPUs, and the critical section nobody guarded
stages.predict: What a spinning CPU and a deferred one have in common, and what the same schedule scores with a lock and without one.

stages.title: The format, and the write that was not ordered
stages.predict: Which sector has to be written last for an interrupted format to leave nothing to mount, and what a checksum per sector buys a filesystem that a power failure can tear.

stages.title: The capstone: the userland, and the kernel's own ledger
stages.predict: What two records have to agree about before a kernel may be believed, and what the frame pool proves that a ledger cannot.

G7.title: Shell From Scratch
G7.why: A shell is what a kernel looks like from the outside: a line of text becomes a process tree, and every promise G4's kernel makes is on show — what a child inherits, what a pipe costs, who waits for whom, and what a signal does to a job. Parse a line into words and operators; expand variables, tilde, globs and here-documents in the order a shell must; fork, exec and wait for real exit codes; build pipes and redirections as a descriptor table before anything runs; keep a job table that knows a background job from a stopped one; send signals and reap a child without losing it; and end on a session the harness replays byte for byte, where `set -e`, `&&` and a pipeline's exit status are decided by the rules and not by luck. Author shell-from-scratch against the kernel of G4.

G8.title: Runtime From Scratch
G8.why: A language runtime makes two promises — the program runs, and memory stops being your problem — and a provided bytecode, assembler and heap are where you keep both. Execute a stack machine with calls, frames and exact step accounting; lay out a heap of objects with headers and references; then collect, in the order the field settled it: mark and sweep, reference counting that cannot free a cycle, a tri-colour incremental collector that must not lose an object the mutator can still reach, write barriers and a remembered set, a nursery, and a copying collector that moves objects without breaking a reference. The acceptance is a program's own output plus its collection counts, and the one invariant a collector may never break: nothing reachable is ever collected, and no uncollected frame is ever read. Author runtime-from-scratch.

G9.title: Coreutils From Scratch
G9.why: The tools the terminal is made of, each one a byte-oriented contract: grep is a matcher whose anchors, classes and -v inversion are decisions, not flags; tail is circulation over a fixed buffer for -n and a backward scan for -c, and its -f is a polling loop the harness drives tick by tick; sort's merge and key spec; wc's count that must be wrong the same way GNU is wrong when the last line lacks its newline; and an editor that is a gap buffer, a screen model of rows and columns over those bytes, and the redraw that shows exactly the cursor's truth. Each command is judged byte-for-byte against the real one on provided corpora, the editor against scripted keystrokes and the frame it must have drawn. Author coreutils-from-scratch; nothing must come first — bytes and integers the whole way.

G10.title: Custom OS in C, End to End
G10.why: The big one, and the only project in this repository where the acceptance is real hardware obeying you: a bootable x86-64 kernel in C and a userland on top, built end to end — GRUB or your own bootloader handing control at the magic number, the GDT and IDT you write by hand, the PIT and the APIC and the timer that makes time exist, physical and virtual memory with the page tables QEMU's `info page-tables` can show you, interrupts where a keypress becomes a scan code becomes a character on your own screen, the scheduler you proved as data in G4 now context-switching for real, the syscall entry with its privilege ring crossing and the user pointer you must validate twice, drivers written against the device rather than a model: the PS/2 controller's ports and its second-byte wait, the ATA identify and the read sector that polls its status register, PCI enumeration walking the config space bus by bus, and the e1000 or virtio NIC whose ring you fill and whose interrupt you share; a ramdisk and then a real filesystem on a disk image, an ELF loader so a program you compiled with G5 runs as a process with its own address space, fork and exec and wait as real code, and the shell from G7 speaking to your kernel instead of another's. QEMU is the judge where the checker can reach (`info registers`, the serial log, the framebuffer the test draws to); the real machine is the honest one. The graded path is the x86-64 stages; the arm64 port is the second half. Author custom-os-from-scratch in C; G4's simulator is the model, G5 the toolchain, linux-from-scratch/ the prose.

G11.title: Advanced Algorithms & Data Structures
G11.why: La Rocca's book mechanised, one stage per chapter, every structure judged against a work counter and a reference the way B2 judges HNSW against brute force: priority queues and d-way heaps measured on Dijkstra (ch. 2), treaps where the rotation is right because the expected height the profiler prints agrees with the theory (ch. 3), Bloom filters whose false-positive rate is measured, not assumed, against the exact set (ch. 4), disjoint sets by path compression and union by rank counted in finds (ch. 5), tries and T9 and autocomplete with the compressed variant (ch. 6), LRU and LFU caches with the hit rate the workload produces (ch. 7), k-d trees whose nearest neighbour is checked against the linear scan it must beat (ch. 8–9), SS-trees and approximate search with the recall the book's own image retrieval asks for (ch. 10–11), DBSCAN and OPTICS clustering on the points the reference clusters identically (ch. 12–13), graphs from BFS and connected components to Dijkstra and minimum spanning trees (ch. 14), graph embeddings, planarity and the force-directed drawing whose crossings the checker counts (ch. 15), then gradient descent (ch. 16) and simulated annealing (ch. 17) as optimisation on those graphs, and the genetic algorithm that closes the book on TSP, its tours compared against the branch-and-bound answer on the small instances (ch. 18). Author advanced-dsa-from-scratch in pure Python with no float where a counter suffices — nothing must come first; the book is the reading, the checker the grade.

H1.title: Distributed Training
H1.why: Built: the plans on top of I9's collectives, on a fabric copied verbatim and a model handed to you. A step as a plan with its bytes per rank and its memory ledger, DDP's bucketed all-reduce hidden behind the compute, ZeRO's ladder (4 + 12/N, then 2 + 2/N + 12/N), FSDP's per-unit gather and scatter and its 4P(N-1)/N peak, tensor parallel's two all-reduces per block, GPipe vs 1F1B and the bubble replayed from the slots, interleaving's (p-1)/(m*v+p-1), the expert all-to-all with its routing table and capacity cap, ring attention's exact running pivot, and the configuration whose report is recomputed from the plan it chose. 10 checks, 554 mutations caught, no float anywhere.

H5.title: Query Engine From Scratch
H5.why: A database is a file format plus a promise about what a query returns. A heap file of pages on a disk that can lose what was not synced, a catalog, and tables to query are provided. Parse a SQL subset into a tree; resolve names against a catalog that may be wrong; plan it — predicate pushdown, join order, an index chosen or refused; execute with iterators over a page buffer and a B+tree you split yourself; make a transaction a log and a commit a rule; and prove it: the same rows as the reference for a hundred queries, a plan that uses the index only when the predicate earns it, and a crash schedule where the log decides which tuples exist. Author query-engine-from-scratch; G4 is the format and the barrier, and A6 is the distributed half this repo already has.

H6.title: Consensus From Scratch
H6.why: Consensus is the one thing a replicated system cannot fake: a leader is a number a majority agreed on, and a log entry is committed when a majority holds it. Five nodes, a deterministic network with partitions and delays, a clock, and durable storage that can lose its last write are provided. Elect a leader with terms and votes; replicate a log whose entries match term by term; commit only what a majority holds and refuse a stale leader; keep a membership change safe; snapshot a log without losing a committed entry; and recover a node whose disk lied. The acceptance is a linearizability check over the history the world itself recorded, plus a partition schedule on which the wrong implementation splits the brain. Author consensus-from-scratch; J3 is durability and I9 is the fabric.

H7.title: Compression From Scratch
H7.why: A compressor is a byte format you can be exactly wrong about, and it is judged on a ratio: Huffman with canonical codes and a length limit; LZ77's window and why its size is the whole trade; LZ4's block format with its nibble lengths; DEFLATE bit by bit — dynamic trees, the matched pairs, the end-of-block symbol, and the stored/static/dynamic choice per block; then FSE/ANS with a table you build, and a frame with a real header and a checksum. The reference decoders (inflate, LZ4, a zstd-compatible frame reader) and the corpora are provided. A stage passes when the decoder accepts your bytes and the ratio clears the bar, and the tester flips one bit to see whether the checksum you wrote notices. Author compression-from-scratch; nothing to read first — it is bytes and integers the whole way.

H8.title: Multi-Region Failover
H8.why: A replica is not a strategy until you have failed it over: the region that answers has to be a decision with a rule, the write that arrived late has to be reconciled rather than guessed at, and the RTO you claim has to be a number your own drill produced. Two simulated regions with independent clocks, a link that drops for a chosen window, and clients with pinned sessions are provided. Write the health signal that is not a heartbeat, the promotion rule with both of its halves — H6's quorum and A6's hinted handoff and Merkle anti-entropy — the redirect that does not apply a write twice, and the report that states RTO and RPO as measured, with the writes it lost named. Author failover-from-scratch; A6 and H6 are the two halves it joins.

I1.why: The silicon half: thread blocks, warps and SIMT divergence are G1's 12 checks; then author gpu-architecture-from-scratch for the memory hierarchy (banks, coalescing, TLB, PCIe vs NVLink) and the matmul kernel, as a simulator plus a roofline, with the CUDA/cuBLAS profile as the runbook. Deterministic and in-process over a provided fabric (links with bandwidth and latency, four topologies, an executor): a collective is a plan whose correctness and whose price are checked separately, with 438 planted mutations behind the ten checks. The prerequisite for H1, the distributed-training course.

I13.title: Serving Cluster From Scratch
I13.why: The last mile of serving is not a model, it is a cluster that stays ready: a supervisor that brings a rank back without losing the mesh, readiness that means the weights are in VRAM rather than the process is alive, and a drain that finishes the requests it already accepted instead of dropping them at the load balancer. I14.why: Cold starts are usually a storage problem wearing compute clothes: getting the right shard onto the node is the bring-up cost, and every byte fetched eagerly is paid again on every replica. Write the manifest and its digests, the shard-to-rank map, the lazy load with a prefetch order derived from the first tokens, the CDN layer whose cache key is the digest and whose invalidation is a new digest, and the measurement that says which of those actually cut cold start — bytes fetched, time to first token, cache hit rate per node. J3.title: Durable Execution
J3.why: Built and ready: a run as a log rather than a process. The line and the journal that holds it, the write that was not synced and the sync that makes it a fact, replay with the half-written tail refused rather than guessed at, a lease whose deadline is derived from the line and whose owner is named, the heartbeat and the grace that separate *expired* from *dead*, a crash that replays only what the disk would keep and writes the lines the dead owners' jobs owe, an effect that happens exactly once because its intent is synced before it runs, a checkpoint and a resume that refuses another run's log by name, a report whose every counter is recounted from the lines, and a capstone that kills one worker holding a lease in the middle of the run and still lands on the same states as the run nobody killed. 10 checks and 558 mutations caught, on a disk that loses everything it was not told to sync: no threads, no filesystem, no floats.

K6.title: Forward Deployed Engineer
K6.why: The twelve skills an FDE is hired for, as twelve stages against a customer that is data: the assertion, the session and the row; a deployment that cannot reach out; an invoice feed reconciled into a hybrid store; a retriever that filters before the limit; the legacy system as tools with the credential staying in the vault; PII masked on the way out and restored on the way back; a workflow that stops at a person and journals the decision; the model that fits the GPU somebody else owns; the AI's work counted in hours and cents; the customer's own tickets run in shadow and answered with one verdict; a vague ask turned into a scoped four weeks; and a runbook drilled against armed faults, handed to an admin who is not you. M0.title: Credit Origination
M0.why: Before a loan exists it is an application, and the bank's first arithmetic is a decision: the applicant as facts (income, obligations, collateral, history) on a provided estate that is the ground truth, the affordability ratio and the debt-service math that says whether the payment fits, the application scorecard — weight, points, cutoff — as a table a reviewer can audit rather than a model they must trust, the rating the bank assigns and the price it sets from it (the rate that covers expected loss plus funding plus capital charge, in basis points), the limit structure and what is committed versus uncommitted, the collateral and its haircuts and lien, the covenant as a promise written before the drawdown, the approval as a record with who decided and why, and the offer letter the contract then becomes. Ends where M1 begins: a booked facility with its schedule. Author credit-origination-from-scratch; nothing must come first — the decision is integer arithmetic and a policy, not a model.

M3.title: Collections, Workout and Recovery
M3.why: The loan after it goes wrong, as actions and their consequences over M1's own book and ledger: the delinquency strategy as a state machine (dunning at day X, call at day Y, referral at day Z, each step a record the customer's own history answers), forbearance as the bank's decision — the restructure, the term extension, the capitalisation of arrears — and the probation and cure it triggers, the cure rate and the re-default the strategy is measured on, the collections waterfall over the cash that arrives (what pays fees, what pays interest, what pays principal, and what the ledger says actually happened), the workout on default: the sale of the collateral and its costs, the settlement, the deficiency that survives, the write-off as an accounting act distinct from the cash recovery that follows it, the recovery cash flows M1's stage 4 discounted — now produced by the strategy you wrote and measured against the bank's actuals, and the per-loan story: one loan followed from first missed payment to final recovery, every bank action and cash movement on its own line. Author collections-workout-from-scratch; M1 is the book and the default definition it works on.

M4.title: Bank P&L and the Loan's Full Cost
M4.why: Where the contract lands on the bank's own statements, over M1's book with the strategy M3 wrote: the interest income the schedule earns and the day-count that computes it, the funding cost of every euro lent (the transfer price, in basis points, and why a 300bp margin is not 300bp of profit), the expected loss booked as the provision (M1's stage 6) and the release or charge as stages move, the impairment P&L line the roll-forward explains, the unexpected loss the capital absorbs and the return on it — RAROC as a ratio of exact integers, the operating cost of the origination (M0) and collections (M3) machinery, fee income and its recognition, the economic profit per loan, grade and vintage, and the statement the course files: for the same book, the net interest, the provision charge, the cost and the capital — the numbers a chief credit officer reads and the per-grade report that shows where the bank made money and where the contract's risk ate it. Author bank-pl-from-scratch; M1 is the book, M3 the cash that actually arrives.

M2.title: IRB and Regulatory Capital
M2.why: The bank's own estimates, and the ones the regulator does not let it trust alone: the PIT/TTC split and where each is legal, the IRB risk-weight formula as integer arithmetic — the correlation R per asset class, the maturity adjustment, the capital requirement K as the exact series it is, the normal quantile tabulated as data because the house rule is no float and a table is also what a reviewer can recompute — downturn LGD (the downturn multiplier and the collateral it is allowed to haircut), best-estimate LGD for the accounting stage against the downturn floor for the capital stage, BE-EAD with its CCFs, the output floor phased in over the schedule, and the reconcile-the-two-books check: IFRS 9's provision and IRB's capital computed from the same world, per grade and in total, each shown where the other cannot agree with it. Author irb-capital-from-scratch over M1's book, dates and rules, with the policy extended rather than replaced and every number still basis points.

M5.title: Distressed Debt Investing
M5.why: The same default seen from the buy side, where it is an opportunity with a price: the capital structure as a waterfall of claims over M1's borrower — who is owed what, secured ahead of whom — the distressed bond and loan bought below par, and the question every price asks: recovery, reorganisation, or the debtor's death; the distressed exchange and the maturity extension as the negotiated outcomes, the restructuring waterfall applied to the absolute-priority rule and the violations that settle it in practice, the claim the fund bought valued three ways — the expected recovery from M3's actual cash flows, the Merton distance-to-default on the borrower's own assets, and the comparables — and where the three disagree is the trade; the entry price implied return and the IRR in basis points that survives the timing of the recovery, the hold decision against the carry, and the report the fund writes: why this claim, at this price, with what recovery and by when — checked against what actually happened to the borrower. Author distressed-debt-from-scratch over M1's book and M3's collections log; the bank's provisioning and the fund's thesis are two readings of one default.

N1.title: Blockchain From Scratch
N1.why: A ledger is a hash chain plus a rule for who appends: the block header and the digest that seals it, Merkle trees and the inclusion proof that is the point of them, addresses and signatures over a provided keypair scheme, the UTXO set and the spend that must name what it consumes, the mempool and the double-spend the ordering kills, proof-of-work's target and difficulty adjustment as the two constants that make a chain honest about time, then proof-of-stake's slots and attestations on the same world, fork choice as a rule recomputable from any node's own view, and a network of simulated peers whose clocks and drops the harness drives — accepted when every node converges on the same chain and a planted fork with less honest weight loses. Author blockchain-from-scratch; H6 is the agreement half taken seriously, N1 the ledger half.

N2.title: Smart Contracts & dApp
N2.why: A contract is a program the ledger agrees to run exactly once, priced by the work it does: the account model over N1's UTXO world, the bytecode VM — stack, memory, storage whose every cold slot is charged — and the gas schedule that makes the meter real; a compiler from a toy contract language to that bytecode with the ABI that lets a caller encode a call; the escrow, the token and the voting contracts written in it, each with the reentrancy or overflow bug the tester plants and the checker asks your guard about; then the dApp on top: a local node your client talks to, transactions signed, sent and receipted, events indexed by your own scanner, and the front-end state machine that reads the chain and never trusts it. Author dapp-from-scratch; N1 is the machine it runs on.

N3.title: MuJoCo-Style Physics Engine
N3.why: A physics engine is a constraint solver wearing a scene graph: rigid bodies with mass and inertia tensors, contact detection as narrowphase over provided shapes, the contact Jacobian and the LCP that a projected solver iterates to rest, the warm start that makes it stable, the integrator's order and its energy drift, actuators and PD control, then a MuJoCo-shaped MJCF subset parsed into that world — and the proof of the whole thing: the gradients. MuJoCo exists because differentiable simulation trains controllers; A8's exact reverse mode over the solver's unrolled steps is the capstone, checked against the finite-difference oracle at every parameter. Author physics-engine-from-scratch; A8 is the engine that makes the last stage possible.
